why.correct: Total body water = 0.60 × 80 kg = 48 L. Intracellular fluid is about two thirds of that: 48 × 2/3 = 32 L.
options: 16 L is one third of 48 L, which is the extracellular fluid, not the intracellular fluid.
48 L is his total body water. Only part of it is inside cells.
Correct. Two thirds of 48 L is 32 L.
24 L is half of 48 L. The intracellular share is two thirds, not half.

why.correct: Total body water = 0.50 × 60 = 30 L. ECF is one third: 10 L. Plasma is one quarter of the ECF: 2.5 L.
options: 10 L is her whole extracellular fluid. Plasma is only one quarter of it.
7.5 L is her interstitial fluid, the three quarters of the ECF outside the blood vessels.
5 L is roughly an adult's whole blood volume, which includes the cells. The question asks for plasma, which works out at 2.5 L here.

why.correct: The fluid in the spaces between the cells, outside both the cells and the capillary, is interstitial fluid. It is the larger part of the extracellular fluid, about three quarters of it.
options: Correct. The fluid between cells is interstitial fluid.
Plasma is the fluid inside the capillary, not the fluid between the cells.
Intracellular fluid is inside the cells, bounded by their plasma membranes.

why.correct: Only the intracellular fluid bars show low sodium with high potassium, phosphate and protein. The sodium–potassium pump keeps sodium out of cells and potassium in, and phosphates and proteins are trapped inside.
options: On the graph, plasma is high in sodium and low in potassium (about 140 and 4 to 5 in a real blood test), the reverse of this sample.
Interstitial fluid is high in sodium and chloride and low in potassium and protein.
Correct. Low sodium, high potassium and lots of phosphate and protein mark intracellular fluid.
Both extracellular fluids are high in sodium and low in potassium, so no mixture of them could give this sample.

why.correct: Plasma and interstitial fluid are separated by capillary walls. Small ions cross freely through the gaps between endothelial cells, so their concentrations even out; plasma proteins mostly cannot cross, so they stay in the plasma.
options: Correct. A barrier permeable to small ions but not to proteins gives exactly this pattern.
Cells do not pump protein into the plasma. Most plasma proteins are made by the liver and released into the blood, and they stay there because capillary walls hold them back.
Some interstitial protein is returned to the blood by lymph, but breakdown by cells does not explain why the ions match. The barrier does.
Ions even out across capillary walls because they cross freely, not because a pump sets them.
A loss of 0.5 L comes from leaving out the 0.3 L of metabolic water, which is a real gain made inside cells.
Intake and output do not match here: 2.3 L in and 2.5 L out.
This reverses the sign. Output is larger than intake, so she loses water.
Correct. 2.3 L in, 2.5 L out: a loss of 0.2 L.

why.correct: Insensible losses are the ones you do not notice: water evaporating through the epidermis and water vapor leaving in each breath. Together they are about 0.7 L a day at rest.
options: Yes. Air leaving the lungs is saturated with water vapor.
No. Sweat is a separate, visible loss controlled by the body temperature loop.
Yes. Water diffuses through the epidermis and evaporates, separately from sweat.
No. Urine is a sensible loss, and the one the kidneys adjust.
No. Fecal water is a small but sensible loss.

why.correct: Pure water dilutes every compartment and enters cells. The fall in plasma osmolality shuts off ADH through the osmoreceptors, the collecting ducts lose their aquaporins, and a large volume of dilute urine removes the extra water over the next few hours.

variables.name: Plasma osmolality
variables.why: The water is absorbed and adds no solute, so the same solute is spread through more water.

variables.name: Intracellular fluid volume
variables.why: The more dilute extracellular fluid is hypotonic to cells, so water moves into them until osmolality is equal again.

variables.name: ADH release
variables.why: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors swell and fire less when plasma osmolality falls, so the posterior pituitary releases less ADH.

variables.name: Water permeability of the collecting ducts
variables.why: With little ADH, principal cells pull their aquaporins back into vesicles, so the ducts become nearly waterproof.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: Water stays in the collecting ducts instead of being reabsorbed, so much more urine is made.

variables.name: Urine osmolality
variables.why: The dilute fluid leaving the loop is not concentrated further in the collecting duct, so urine can fall toward 50 mOsm/L.

why.correct: Salt raises plasma osmolality, which draws water out of the osmoreceptors. They fire faster and drive ADH release from the posterior pituitary. ADH makes principal cells insert aquaporins, water is reabsorbed, osmolality falls back, and the osmoreceptors ease off: negative feedback.
Osmoreceptors drive hypothalamic neurons whose axons end in the posterior pituitary. They release ADH, which acts on principal cells to insert aquaporins.
options: Correct. ADH from the posterior pituitary is the link between osmoreceptors and aquaporins.
Aldosterone makes principal cells keep sodium and secrete potassium. It does not insert aquaporins, and osmoreceptors do not drive it.
ANP is released when the atria are stretched, and it makes the kidneys excrete sodium and water, the opposite of this step.
Renin starts the RAAS in response to low pressure or volume. It is not the step that follows osmoreceptor firing.

why.correct: He has lost more water than solute, so his ECF is more concentrated than his cells. Water follows the solute out of the cells, and they shrink. Shrinking brain cells cause his confusion.
options: Cells swell when the ECF becomes more dilute, as in water intoxication. His plasma is concentrated, so water leaves cells.
Correct. Hypertonic ECF draws water out of cells, including neurons.
Cells keep their size only when a loss is isotonic, as in bleeding. His plasma is concentrated with sodium, which stays outside cells, so water leaves them.
The blood–brain barrier restricts many solutes, but water crosses it and brain cell membranes, so brain cells respond to plasma osmolality.

why.correct: An isotonic loss removes salt and water together from the ECF. Osmolality does not change, so no water moves across plasma membranes. Only the ECF shrinks: this is hypovolemia.
options: That is the pattern of losing more water than solute. An isotonic loss leaves osmolality unchanged.
Osmolality falls only when water is gained or solute is lost in excess of water.
Losses spread across all compartments only when pure water is lost. Water moves into or out of cells only when ECF osmolality changes.
Correct. Isotonic loss shrinks the ECF alone. (If she drank plain water to replace it, her plasma would become dilute.)

why.correct: Once the glucose is used, 1 L of free water remains, and it spreads through total body water: two thirds into cells, one third (333 mL) into the ECF. Plasma is a quarter of the ECF: 333 ÷ 4 ≈ 83 mL.
options: 250 mL is what stays in the plasma from 1 L of isotonic saline, which stays entirely in the ECF. D5W's free water also enters cells.
Correct. One third to the ECF, one quarter of that to the plasma: about 83 mL.
333 mL is the ECF share. Three quarters of it goes to the interstitial fluid, not the plasma.
The water does not stay in the vessels: it crosses capillary walls and plasma membranes.

why.correct: Total solute = 290 × 42 = 12,180 mOsm. Water adds no solute, so the new osmolality = 12,180 ÷ 44 ≈ 277 mOsm/kg.
options: Correct. The same solute in 44 L instead of 42 L gives about 277 mOsm/kg.
304 would mean the fluid became more concentrated. Adding water dilutes it.
Osmolality stays at 290 only if the drink carries solute at the same concentration, as with isotonic saline. Plain water dilutes it.
145 would mean the water doubled. Two liters added to 42 changes the volume by less than 5%.

why.correct: Constant ADH (SIADH) makes his kidneys keep water although his plasma is dilute. He has gained water in excess of solute, so ECF osmolality falls, water moves into cells, and swelling brain cells inside the rigid skull cause headache and confusion.
options: Dehydration raises plasma osmolality. His is low, at 255.
Hypovolemia is an isotonic loss with normal osmolality. His osmolality is low and he is keeping water, not losing it.
Correct. Water gain lowers osmolality and swells cells; the brain has no room to swell.
Hypervolemia is an isotonic gain with normal osmolality, and it causes edema by raising capillary pressure. His problem is dilute plasma.

why.correct: Sensory receptors in the mouth and throat report swallowed water to the hypothalamus, which damps thirst before any water is absorbed. This early signal limits drinking while the first water is still in the gut.
options: Water in the stomach has not yet entered the blood, so it cannot change plasma osmolality there.
ADH acts on the kidneys, not on the thirst center, and it falls rather than rises as thirst is satisfied.
Correct. The early shut-off comes from the mouth and throat.
The kidneys respond to the water only after it is absorbed, and they do not signal the thirst center.

why.correct: Losing dilute sweat raises plasma osmolality and lowers ECF volume. Water leaves cells, and both the osmolality and volume triggers raise ADH, renin and thirst. The kidneys save water, but only drinking can replace the 2 L lost.

variables.name: Plasma osmolality
variables.why: Sweat is more dilute than plasma, so she loses more water than solute and her plasma becomes more concentrated.

variables.name: Intracellular fluid volume
variables.why: The more concentrated ECF draws water out of cells, so they shrink.

variables.name: ADH release
variables.why: Osmoreceptors shrink and fire faster, and the fall in blood volume adds a second push for ADH release.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: ADH inserts aquaporins in the collecting ducts, so more water is reabsorbed and little urine is made.

variables.name: Renin release
variables.why: Plasma volume falls, so pressure in the kidney's small arteries falls and sympathetic activity rises, both of which increase renin release.

variables.name: Thirst
variables.why: The rise in osmolality acts on the osmoreceptors, and angiotensin II from the RAAS adds to it, stimulating the thirst center.

why.correct: Hypervolemia comes from keeping or receiving salt and water together: heart failure (the kidneys keep salt and water), kidney failure (they cannot excrete it), and excess isotonic IV fluid. Sweating and diabetes insipidus remove water.
options: Yes. A failing heart leaves the kidneys underperfused, and they keep salt and water through the RAAS.
No. Sweat loss without drinking removes more water than salt: dehydration.
Yes. Failing kidneys cannot excrete the salt and water taken in.
No. Without ADH action, the kidneys lose large volumes of water: dehydration if the person cannot drink enough.
Yes. Isotonic saline stays in the ECF and expands it.

why.correct: When plasma osmolality rises, water leaves the osmoreceptors, following the solute outside, so they shrink, not swell. Shrinking is what makes them fire faster.
options: This step is right. Sweat is more dilute than plasma, so losing it concentrates the plasma.
This is the error. Osmoreceptors shrink in concentrated plasma; they swell only when the plasma becomes dilute.
This step is right. Faster osmoreceptor firing drives ADH release.
This step is right. ADH makes principal cells insert aquaporins.
This step is right. With water reabsorbed, the urine is small in volume and concentrated.

why.correct: With less muscle, an older adult's total body water is a smaller share of body mass, so 2 L is a larger fraction of it and raises osmolality more. Thirst is also blunted with age, so they drink less to correct it.
options: Fat tissue holds little water. Having more fat and less muscle lowers the share of body water, the opposite of what this option implies.
Correct. A smaller water reserve and weaker thirst both raise the risk.
The reverse is closer to the truth: ageing kidneys concentrate urine less well, so they save water less effectively.
Older adults still lose water insensibly through the epidermis and in exhaled air, as everyone does.

why.correct: 8 mg/dL = 80 mg/L. Divide by 40 mg per mmol: 80 ÷ 40 = 2.0 mmol/L.
options: 0.2 comes from dividing 8 by 40 without converting deciliters to liters. There are 10 dL in a liter.
Correct. 80 mg/L ÷ 40 mg/mmol = 2.0 mmol/L.
4.0 is the value in mEq/L: calcium carries two charges, so 2.0 mmol/L is 4.0 mEq/L. The question asks for mmol/L.
1.0 comes from dividing by calcium's two charges. The charge converts mmol to mEq, and it multiplies: 2.0 mmol/L is 4.0 mEq/L.

why.correct: She gained about 2 L of water, and exercise and nausea kept her ADH high, so her kidneys could not pass it. The same sodium is diluted in more water. Hyponatremia is almost always too much water for the sodium present.
options: She did lose some sodium in sweat, but sweat is more dilute than plasma. That loss alone would raise, not lower, her plasma sodium concentration.
Nothing suggests aldosterone failed, and losing aldosterone takes days to lower sodium. Her problem developed over hours from drinking.
Correct. A net gain of water dilutes her plasma sodium.
Her kidneys were keeping, not wasting, what they could; with ADH high they could not excrete the extra water.

why.correct: Normal plasma sodium is about 135 to 145 mmol/L. Above 145 is hypernatremia, so 152 qualifies.
options: 128 is below 135: that is hyponatremia.
138 is in the normal range.
144 is at the top of the normal range, not above it.
Correct. 152 is above 145 mmol/L.

why.correct: Fever raises her insensible water loss, and she cannot respond to thirst by drinking. She has lost water, so her plasma sodium is concentrated. Hypernatremia almost always means a water deficit.
options: Correct. Water losses without water intake raise the sodium concentration.
Nothing in her story points to extra salt, and a person with normal kidneys excretes extra dietary sodium. The rise comes from lost water.
Aldosterone makes the kidneys keep salt and water together, which mainly raises volume. It rarely raises sodium above 145.
SIADH makes the kidneys keep water, which lowers plasma sodium, the opposite of her result.

why.correct: Over about two days, brain cells in dilute plasma shed potassium and small organic solutes, so they stop swelling. If plasma sodium then rises quickly, water rushes out of these adapted cells and they are damaged, especially the myelin in the pons: osmotic demyelination. Slow correction gives them time to regain solute.
options: Healthy kidneys can excrete water much faster than this. The limit protects the brain, not the kidneys.
Raising sodium from 112 by 8 a day would take days to reach even the low normal range. Overshooting to above 145 is not the concern.
Correct. Adapted brain cells shrink too fast when the plasma is concentrated quickly.
IV salt enters the plasma at once. The limit on speed is chosen by the doctors, not set by delivery.
155 comes from forgetting to double the sodium. Each sodium ion is matched by an anion, so sodium counts twice.
280 counts the sodium and glucose but leaves out urea.
478 comes from adding glucose and urea nitrogen in mg/dL (270 + 180 + 28) without dividing them. They must be converted to mmol/L first.

why.correct: 2% of 3,500 mmol = 70 mmol. Spread through 14 L: 70 ÷ 14 = 5.0 mmol/L added. 4.0 + 5.0 = 9.0 mmol/L, which is life-threatening.
options: This treats the release as a tiny change. Because the ECF holds so little potassium, 70 mmol is more than it held to begin with.
6.5 is the result for a 1% release (35 mmol ÷ 14 L = 2.5 added). The question says 2%.
Correct. 70 mmol ÷ 14 L = 5.0 mmol/L added to 4.0.
74 adds the 70 mmol to the concentration without dividing by the volume.

why.correct: Insulin shifts potassium into cells through the sodium–potassium pump. Plasma potassium falls within minutes, protecting the heart, but the body still holds the same total potassium, so it must still be removed by the kidneys, a binder or dialysis. The glucose is given so the insulin does not cause low blood glucose.

variables.name: Sodium–potassium pump activity in muscle and liver cells
variables.why: Insulin stimulates the sodium–potassium pump, so cells take up more potassium.

variables.name: Plasma potassium
variables.why: Potassium moves from the ECF into cells, so the plasma concentration falls.

variables.name: Total body potassium
variables.why: Insulin only moves potassium between compartments; none has left the body yet.

variables.name: Resting membrane potential of heart cells (how negative)
variables.why: With less potassium outside, the gradient is restored and the resting potential moves back to a more negative value, further from threshold.

why.correct: Hypokalemia comes from losing potassium from the gut, from more distal sodium and flow driving potassium secretion (loop and thiazide diuretics), or from too much aldosterone. ACE inhibitors, kidney failure and crush injury all raise potassium.
options: Yes. Gut fluids carry potassium, and the volume loss also raises aldosterone.
Yes. More sodium and fluid reach the principal cells, so they secrete more potassium.
No. ACE inhibitors lower angiotensin II and aldosterone, so less potassium is secreted: they tend to raise it.
Yes. Excess aldosterone makes principal cells secrete more potassium.
No. Failing kidneys cannot secrete potassium, so it rises.
No. Damaged muscle cells release their potassium into the ECF, raising it.

why.correct: Hyperkalemia moves the resting potential of heart cells toward threshold. Raising extracellular calcium raises the threshold, restoring the gap between rest and threshold. It buys 30 to 60 minutes while insulin and glucose shift potassium into cells and dialysis removes it. It does not lower potassium.
options: Correct. Calcium stabilizes the heart's membranes without changing potassium.
Calcium and potassium are both cations and do not bind each other; his potassium is unchanged.
Calcium does not drive potassium secretion, and his kidneys have failed anyway.
Calcium does not shift potassium into cells. That is what insulin, glucose and beta-2 agonists do.

why.correct: With less potassium outside, the concentration gradient is steeper, more potassium leaks out, and the resting potential becomes more negative. The fibers sit further from threshold, so stronger stimuli are needed and the muscles are weak.
options: Moving toward threshold is what a rise in potassium does, not a fall.
Correct. Hypokalemia hyperpolarizes muscle fibers.
The pump cannot restore a gradient that is set by the low plasma potassium; the resting potential follows the gradient.
No change in potassium reverses the resting potential. The inside stays negative.

why.correct: Aldosterone acts on principal cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct, not the proximal tubule. That is where potassium is secreted into the urine.
options: This step is right. The ECF holds little potassium, so a meal raises it quickly.
This step is right. Insulin stimulates sodium–potassium pumps, which move potassium into cells.
This step is right. Potassium acts directly on the zona glomerulosa.
This is the error. Aldosterone's targets are the principal cells, far along the tubule; the proximal tubule reabsorbs potassium.
This step is right. Principal cells secrete the extra potassium, restoring balance.

why.correct: Hyperventilation blows off CO₂, so the blood becomes alkaline. In alkalosis, albumin gives up hydrogen ions and binds more calcium, so ionized calcium falls although the total is unchanged. Low ionized calcium makes nerves and muscles overexcitable: tingling and cramps.
options: Calcium is not a gas and does not leave in exhaled air. Breathing changes CO₂, which changes pH.
PTH takes minutes to hours to act, and panic does not switch it off. Her total calcium is normal.
Nothing like this happens in minutes, and her total calcium has not fallen.
Correct. Only the free fraction falls, so the total calcium looks normal.

why.correct: 4.0 − 2.5 = 1.5. 0.8 × 1.5 = 1.2. 7.8 + 1.2 = 9.0 mg/dL, in the normal range, suggesting the low total may reflect her low albumin. The formula is only an estimate; ionized calcium settles it.
options: 6.6 subtracts the correction. Low albumin means less calcium is bound, so the correction is added.
11.0 uses the albumin value itself (0.8 × 4.0) instead of the shortfall from 4.0.
7.8 is the measured value before adjusting for the low albumin.

why.correct: Failing kidneys keep phosphate and make less calcitriol, so calcium falls and PTH rises. The high PTH pulls calcium from bone, weakening it. Potassium tends to rise as secretion falls.

variables.name: Plasma phosphate
variables.why: The kidneys are the main exit for phosphate, so less is filtered and excreted while intake continues.

variables.name: Calcitriol
variables.why: Damaged kidneys make less of the enzyme that activates vitamin D, and high phosphate suppresses it too.

variables.name: Ionized calcium
variables.why: Less calcitriol means less calcium absorbed from food, and high phosphate binds calcium in the blood.

variables.name: PTH
variables.why: Chief cells of the parathyroid glands sense the low calcium and release more PTH.

variables.name: Plasma potassium
variables.why: Fewer working nephrons secrete less potassium, so it tends to build up, especially after potassium-rich meals.

why.correct: Feeding releases insulin, which drives glucose and phosphate into cells, where phosphate is used to make ATP, glycogen and phosphorylated sugars. His stores were already low, so plasma phosphate crashes. Without it, cells cannot make enough ATP, and the diaphragm weakens.
options: Food contains plenty of phosphate. The fall comes from phosphate moving into cells faster than it can be absorbed.
Correct. This is refeeding: an internal shift into cells.
PTH does increase phosphate excretion, but nothing here raised PTH. The fall came within two days of feeding.
Bone mineralization is slow and would not drop phosphate this fast. The fast shift is into cells.

why.correct: Stomach acid is hydrochloric acid, so vomiting removes chloride and hydrogen ions. For every hydrogen ion the parietal cells secreted, one bicarbonate entered the blood. With the acid vomited instead of reaching the intestine, that bicarbonate is never used up, and the low volume and chloride make the kidneys keep it. Chloride falls, bicarbonate rises, and the blood becomes alkaline.
options: The stomach secretes acid, not bicarbonate. Vomiting removes acid, which is why bicarbonate rises, not falls.
Correct. The alkaline tide leaves bicarbonate behind in the blood while chloride leaves in the vomit.
Low chloride does help the kidneys keep the extra bicarbonate, but they do not stop secreting acid. The rise in bicarbonate starts with the stomach.
They are different anions. They move in opposite directions because the vomit carries chloride away while making the acid left bicarbonate in the blood.

why.correct: 0.9% saline contains 154 mmol/L of chloride, against about 100 in plasma. Large volumes raise plasma chloride, and bicarbonate falls, making the blood mildly acidic.
options: Correct. 154 mmol/L is about half again as much as plasma's 100.
Saline has the same osmolality as plasma, so it does not dilute it; and its chloride is higher than plasma's.
Isotonic means the same total particles, not the same mix. Saline has more chloride and no bicarbonate.
The kidneys do excrete some of the load, but not fast enough to prevent the rise during a large infusion.

why.correct: Heavy alcohol use often causes low magnesium. Magnesium normally limits potassium flow out of principal cells; without it, potassium keeps leaking into the urine. Low magnesium also blocks PTH release and action, lowering calcium. Both correct only when magnesium is replaced.
options: Low sodium does not explain potassium that will not correct, or low calcium.
Chloride changes with vomiting and diuretics, but low chloride does not block potassium replacement or PTH.
Correct. Low magnesium keeps potassium and calcium low until it is corrected.
Glucose affects potassium shifts through insulin, but it does not explain both the resistant potassium and the low calcium.

why.correct: High magnesium depresses nerve and muscle, and the tendon reflexes, such as the knee jerk, are lost first, before weakness, slow breathing and cardiac arrest.
options: Correct. Loss of tendon reflexes is the earliest warning.
The pupil response is not the early sign of high magnesium.
Magnesium does not change blood glucose in a way that warns of toxicity.
Skin color changes only late, if breathing fails. It is not the early warning.

why.correct: Potassium is about 140 mEq/L inside cells and under 10 outside, and the ICF is about twice the volume of the ECF. Releasing 1% of the cells' potassium adds several mmol/L to a plasma value of about 4: a large proportional change.
options: Cells hold little sodium, and plasma already has about 140, so a small leak barely changes it.
Cells hold very little chloride, so a leak adds almost none to plasma's 100 or so.
Correct. The steep inside-to-outside difference makes plasma potassium very sensitive to leaks.
Cells hold less bicarbonate than the ECF, so a leak barely changes the plasma value.

why.correct: Dissolved carbon dioxide = 0.03 × 40 = 1.2 mmol/L. The ratio is 24 ÷ 1.2 = 20, and log 20 = 1.3. pH = 6.1 + 1.3 = 7.4.
options: Correct. A ratio of 20 to 1 gives pH 7.40, the middle of the normal range.
7.10 is the pH for a ratio of 10, half the normal ratio. Here the ratio is 20.
7.60 is the pH for a ratio of about 32. That would need more bicarbonate or less carbon dioxide than these values.
6.10 is the pK of the buffer, the number you add the log to. It is the pH only when the ratio is 1.

why.correct: 0.03 × 40 = 1.2 mmol/L dissolved carbon dioxide. The ratio is 12 ÷ 1.2 = 10, and log 10 = 1.0, so pH = 6.1 + 1.0 = 7.1. Halving the ratio lowers pH by 0.3.
options: 7.30 would need a ratio of 16. That is what the ratio becomes if the lungs later lower PCO2 to 25 mm Hg, not before breathing changes.
Correct. Half the bicarbonate at the same PCO2 halves the ratio, from 20 to 10, and pH falls from 7.40 to 7.10.
pH stays 7.40 only if the ratio stays 20. Bicarbonate has halved while carbon dioxide has not changed, so the ratio has halved.
7.20 is the pH for a ratio of 12.5. Halving 20 gives 10, not 12.5.

why.correct: pH depends on the ratio, not the amounts. Patient A: 12 ÷ (0.03 × 20) = 12 ÷ 0.6 = 20. Patient B: 24 ÷ 1.2 = 20. The same ratio gives the same pH, 7.40.
options: Patient A has half the bicarbonate, but also half the carbon dioxide, so the ratio is unchanged and so is the pH.
Correct. Both ratios are 20 to 1, so both pH values are 7.40, even though Patient A's values are both abnormal.
A's carbon dioxide is low, which on its own would raise pH, but his bicarbonate is low by the same proportion, which cancels it.
The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation gives pH from bicarbonate and PCO2 alone. That is how blood gas analyzers relate the three values.

why.correct: Fixed acids that the body cannot burn, such as sulfuric and phosphoric acid, can leave only through the kidneys. Carbonic acid leaves as carbon dioxide, ketone bodies from a fast are burned as fuel, and the acid of a sprint is reversed as liver and muscle burn the lactate.
options: Correct. Sulfur-containing amino acids yield sulfuric acid, which cannot be breathed out or burned. It is the largest share of the daily fixed acid load.
Carbonic acid is the volatile acid. It turns into carbon dioxide, which the lungs breathe out within minutes.
Correct. Phosphoric acid is a fixed acid; the kidneys must excrete it.

Ketone bodies made in a fast are burned by heart, muscle and kidney about as fast as the liver makes them. Blood pH stays close to normal, and they add no lasting acid load for the kidneys to excrete.

The sprint's acid is buffered by bicarbonate and the carbon dioxide is breathed out. Over the next hour or so, the liver and muscles use the lactate as fuel, which takes the hydrogen ions back up. The kidneys hardly need to act.

why.correct: Carbonic anhydrase makes carbonic acid, which splits into H+ and HCO3−. The H+ is pumped into the lumen by an H+-ATPase. There, ammonia takes it up to form ammonium, which is trapped and excreted. The bicarbonate left behind in the cell goes to the blood as new bicarbonate.

Carbonic acid in the lumen does not leave in the urine. Carbonic anhydrase on the brush border splits it into carbon dioxide and water, and the carbon dioxide diffuses into the cell to be used again. The secreted H+ ends up in water, so no acid is excreted in this process.
options: This step is right. Carbonic anhydrase inside the cell makes the H+ and HCO3− that start the cycle.
This step is right. The sodium–hydrogen exchanger swaps H+ out for Na+ in, powered by the sodium gradient.
This is the error. The carbonic acid is split into carbon dioxide and water in the lumen; it is not excreted.
This step is right. The carbon dioxide formed in the lumen crosses into the cell and feeds carbonic anhydrase again.
This step is right. A basolateral carrier moves HCO3− out with Na+, so bicarbonate reaches the blood.

why.correct: The bottom of the ratio is dissolved carbon dioxide: 0.03 mmol/L for each mm Hg of PCO2. At a PCO2 of 40 mm Hg that is 1.2 mmol/L.
options: Correct. 0.03 × PCO2 converts the partial pressure into mmol/L of dissolved carbon dioxide, the same unit as bicarbonate.
Without the 0.03, the two sides of the ratio are in different units, and 24 ÷ 40 would give a pH near 5.9.
Oxygen is not part of the carbonic acid–bicarbonate buffer. The equation uses carbon dioxide.
pH is itself a measure of the hydrogen ion concentration, so it cannot also sit inside the ratio that predicts it.

why.correct: Blocking carbonic anhydrase stops bicarbonate reclaim in the proximal tubule. Bicarbonate spills into the urine, blood bicarbonate and pH fall, and the mild acidity stimulates breathing, which is why the drug helps at altitude.

variables.name: Bicarbonate in the urine
variables.why: Without carbonic anhydrase, the proximal tubule secretes less H+ and cannot turn filtered bicarbonate into carbon dioxide, so filtered bicarbonate stays in the lumen and leaves in the urine.

variables.name: Urine pH
variables.why: The urine now carries extra bicarbonate, a base, so it becomes more alkaline.

variables.name: Plasma bicarbonate
variables.why: Bicarbonate lost in the urine is not replaced, so less remains in the blood.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: Less bicarbonate at the same PCO2 lowers the bicarbonate to carbon dioxide ratio, so pH falls.

why.correct: Bicarbonate buffers the sprint's acid within seconds, and the lungs breathe off the carbon dioxide and push PCO2 below normal. Over the next hour, burning lactate reverses the acid load and restores bicarbonate, with little work for the kidneys.

variables.name: Hydrogen ions in the blood, just after
variables.why: Working muscles release hydrogen ions from splitting glucose and spending ATP faster than they can be handled.

variables.name: Plasma bicarbonate, just after
variables.why: Bicarbonate takes up the extra hydrogen ions, forming carbonic acid and then carbon dioxide, so bicarbonate is used up.

variables.name: Ventilation, just after
variables.why: The carotid bodies sense the lower arterial pH and drive the respiratory centers harder.

variables.name: Arterial PCO2, just after
variables.why: Breathing is driven up faster than carbon dioxide is being made, so more is blown off and PCO2 falls below normal.

variables.name: Plasma bicarbonate, an hour later
variables.why: The liver and muscles use the lactate as fuel, which takes hydrogen ions back up and restores the bicarbonate that was used.

why.correct: Breathing removes only the volatile acid, carbon dioxide. The fixed acids from protein and phosphate compounds can leave only through the kidneys, which also make the new bicarbonate that replaces what those acids use up. Without working kidneys, bicarbonate falls day by day.
options: Correct. Extra breathing can lower PCO2 to keep the ratio closer to normal, but it cannot excrete fixed acid or replace bicarbonate.
The carotid bodies sense arterial pH directly, and kidney failure does not stop them. His breathing does rise a little as his pH falls.
Bicarbonate is an ion dissolved in plasma. It does not leave through the lungs; it is turned into carbon dioxide, which does.
Urea does not block gas exchange. His carbon dioxide leaves normally; the problem is the acid that cannot become a gas.

why.correct: At pH 4.5, [H+] = 10^−4.5 mol/L = 0.000032 mol/L = 0.032 mmol/L. 60 mmol ÷ 0.032 mmol/L ≈ 1,900 L. That is why almost all urinary acid leaves bound to phosphate or ammonia instead.
options: 2 L is a normal daily urine volume. At pH 4.5 it would carry only about 0.06 mmol of free H+.
60 L would follow if each liter held 1 mmol of free H+. At pH 4.5 each liter holds only about 0.03 mmol.
Correct. 60 ÷ 0.032 ≈ 1,900 L, which is why urinary buffers are essential.
190,000 L is a hundred times too large: it treats 10^−4.5 as if it were 10^−6.5.

why.correct: Carbon dioxide production by the cells stays about the same. With less alveolar ventilation, less of it is breathed out each minute, so it builds up in the blood. More carbon dioxide forms more carbonic acid, and pH falls back toward normal.
options: Cells make carbon dioxide according to their metabolism, not according to how fast you breathe.
Correct. Production stays the same while removal falls, so PCO2 rises.
Bicarbonate becomes carbon dioxide only by taking up a hydrogen ion. In alkalosis there are fewer free hydrogen ions, and this is not what the flowchart shows.
Chemoreceptors sense the chemistry of the blood and send nerve signals. They do not release carbon dioxide.

why.correct: The secreted H+ joins filtered bicarbonate to form carbonic acid, which carbonic anhydrase splits into carbon dioxide and water. The H+ ends up in that water. So bicarbonate reclaim stops a loss of base, but it excretes no acid.
options: In this figure every secreted H+ meets a filtered bicarbonate. Free H+ that lowers urine pH comes later, in the collecting duct, after the bicarbonate is gone.
What leaves toward the blood with Na+ is HCO3−, not H+.
Correct. The H+ is recycled into water in the lumen; nothing acidic is excreted.
Ammonium does carry acid out, but the figure does not show ammonia. Here the H+ meets bicarbonate.

why.correct: The bicarbonate buffer is the main buffer of plasma and interstitial fluid. Bicarbonate takes up the H+, forming carbonic acid, which becomes carbon dioxide and water.
options: Plasma holds only about 1 mmol/L of phosphate, too little for much buffering there. Phosphate matters inside cells and in urine.
Ammonia buffers hydrogen ions in the urine, not in plasma.
Intracellular proteins are a large buffer store, but hydrogen ions take minutes to hours to reach them across cell membranes.
Correct. Bicarbonate, at about 24 mmol/L, takes the first hit.

why.correct: Carbon dioxide, its acid end, is removed by the lungs, and bicarbonate, its base end, is adjusted by the kidneys. A buffer whose partners can be topped up or drained keeps working long after a closed buffer would be used up.
options: A buffer's value lies in holding pH steady, not in releasing hydrogen ions. Carbonic acid is a weak acid.
Its pK of 6.1 lies well below blood pH, so on chemistry alone it is a weak buffer at pH 7.4, not a tight binder of hydrogen ions. Its strength lies elsewhere.
Correct. Both partners can be adjusted, which makes it an open system.
Carbonic anhydrase speeds the reaction in whichever direction concentrations push it. It does not change the strength of the acid.

why.correct: Low PCO2 makes her blood alkaline. Low PCO2 also means less H+ forms inside tubule cells, so less bicarbonate is reclaimed, and type B intercalated cells secrete bicarbonate. Losing bicarbonate lowers the top of the ratio to match the lower PCO2, and pH moves back toward normal.
options: More H+ secretion would add new bicarbonate to her blood and make it more alkaline.
Correct. Excreting bicarbonate brings the ratio back toward 20 to 1.
More ammonium excretion adds new bicarbonate to the blood. That is the response to acid, not to alkalinity.
Reclaiming more bicarbonate would keep it in her blood. Her kidneys need to let more go.

why.correct: Carbonic anhydrase made that H+ together with an HCO3− inside the cell. The H+ left in the urine, and the HCO3− crossed into the blood. It replaces a bicarbonate ion that a fixed acid used up.
options: Chloride moves the other way: from the blood into the cell, in exchange for the bicarbonate that leaves.
The hydrogen ion went into the urine. Sending hydrogen ions to the blood is what type B cells do.
Carbon dioxide was used up inside the cell to make the H+ and HCO3−, not added to the blood.
Correct. Every H+ excreted on ammonia or phosphate adds one new bicarbonate to the blood.

why.correct: Filtered load = volume filtered × plasma concentration = 180 L/day × 25 mmol/L = 4,500 mmol/day. Almost all of it must be reclaimed.
options: Correct. 180 × 25 = 4,500 mmol a day, many times the daily fixed acid load.
205 comes from adding 180 and 25. The filtered load is their product.
7.2 comes from dividing 180 by 25. Multiply volume by concentration instead.
45,000 is ten times too large; 180 × 25 is 4,500.

why.correct: Net acid excretion = titratable acid + ammonium − urinary bicarbonate = 20 + 45 − 5 = 60 mmol. In balance, this matches her daily fixed acid production.
options: 70 adds the bicarbonate. Bicarbonate lost in the urine is base, so it is subtracted.
Correct. 20 + 45 − 5 = 60 mmol.
65 leaves out the bicarbonate. Each bicarbonate lost cancels one hydrogen ion excreted.
25 subtracts the ammonium. Ammonium carries acid out, so it is added.

why.correct: Ammonium is the adjustable route. Over 3 to 5 days, the proximal tubule breaks down more glutamine, and ammonium excretion can rise five- to tenfold, adding an equal amount of new bicarbonate to the blood.
options: Correct. Rising ammonium production is the kidneys' main long-term response to an acid load.
Titratable acid is limited by how much phosphate is filtered, so it rises only modestly.
Urine pH cannot fall much below 4.5, where each liter holds only about 0.03 mmol of free H+. Free hydrogen ions carry a tiny share of acid at any pH.
Losing bicarbonate would make his acid load worse. In an acid load the kidneys reclaim essentially all of it.

why.correct: pH 7.26 is acidemia. PaCO2 60 is high, which pushes toward acid and matches the pH, so the disorder is respiratory acidosis. Bicarbonate 26 is still within 22 to 26, so the kidneys have not compensated yet.
options: Partial compensation would need bicarbonate above 26, moving up along with PaCO2. Here it is still normal.
Correct. High PaCO2 explains the low pH, and bicarbonate is still normal: uncompensated.
A metabolic acidosis needs bicarbonate below 22. Here bicarbonate is normal and PaCO2 is what changed.
The pH is low, not high, so this cannot be an alkalosis.

why.correct: pH 7.21 is acidemia. Bicarbonate 7 is very low and matches the acidemia, so the primary disorder is metabolic acidosis. PaCO2 18 has fallen in the same direction, which is her lungs compensating, but pH is still below 7.35: partially compensated.
options: Correct. Low bicarbonate explains the low pH, and the low PaCO2 is her respiratory compensation.
A low PaCO2 alone would raise pH. Her pH is low, so the low PaCO2 is a response, not the cause.
Full compensation would bring pH back to 7.35 to 7.45. Hers is still 7.21.
Respiratory acidosis needs a high PaCO2. Hers is low.

why.correct: pH 7.50 is alkalemia. Bicarbonate 36 is high and pushes toward alkaline, matching the pH: metabolic alkalosis. PaCO2 48 has risen in the same direction, which is the lungs compensating, and pH is still high: partially compensated.
options: The pH is high, so the primary disorder must be an alkalosis. The high PaCO2 is the response, not the cause.
Uncompensated would need a normal PaCO2. At 48 it has risen to compensate.
Correct. High bicarbonate explains the high pH, and PaCO2 has risen partway to match.
Respiratory alkalosis needs a low PaCO2. This PaCO2 is high.

why.correct: The pH is within range but on the alkaline side of 7.40. Low PaCO2 pushes toward alkaline and matches that side, so the primary disorder is respiratory alkalosis, from the extra breathing that low oxygen drives. Bicarbonate has fallen with it, from weeks of kidney bicarbonate loss, and pH is back in range: fully compensated.
options: A normal pH with both numbers abnormal means a disorder and its compensation, not health. Her PaCO2 and bicarbonate are both low.
A primary metabolic acidosis would leave the pH on the acid side of 7.40. Hers is 7.44.
Partial compensation leaves the pH outside 7.35 to 7.45. Hers is inside it.
Correct. Low PaCO2 is primary, low bicarbonate is the renal compensation, and the pH is normal.

why.correct: Anion gap = Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−) = 138 − (100 + 10) = 28 mmol/L, well above the normal 8 to 12. An unmeasured anion has taken bicarbonate's place, so an acid has been added, as in ketoacidosis or lactic acidosis.
options: 12 would be the gap with a normal bicarbonate of 26. Here bicarbonate is 10, so the gap is 28.
Correct. 138 − 110 = 28: a high anion gap metabolic acidosis.
48 comes from adding bicarbonate instead of subtracting it: 138 − 100 + 10.
An acidosis does not change the normal range. A gap of 28 is high whatever the pH.

why.correct: His anion gap is 136 − (114 + 12) = 10 mmol/L: normal. Bicarbonate has fallen and chloride has risen by about the same amount. That pattern means bicarbonate was lost, as happens when intestinal fluid rich in bicarbonate leaves in stool, rather than an acid being added.
options: Ketone body anions would raise the anion gap. His gap is normal.
Lactate is an unmeasured anion too, so lactic acidosis would raise the gap. His is 10.
Correct. A normal gap with high chloride is the signature of bicarbonate loss.
Low bicarbonate is the change here; a respiratory acidosis starts with a high PaCO2, and nothing points to that.

why.correct: Vomiting removes acid and leaves bicarbonate behind, a metabolic alkalosis. The lungs partly compensate by breathing less. Loss of volume, chloride and potassium keeps the kidneys reclaiming bicarbonate instead of excreting it, which is why saline and potassium chloride correct it.

variables.name: Plasma bicarbonate
variables.why: Each H+ her parietal cells secreted sent a bicarbonate into the blood. With the acid vomited, nothing neutralizes that bicarbonate, so it accumulates.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: Higher bicarbonate at first with the same PaCO2 raises the bicarbonate to carbon dioxide ratio, so pH rises.

variables.name: Arterial PaCO2
variables.why: The higher pH slows breathing, so carbon dioxide builds up: respiratory compensation.

variables.name: Plasma chloride
variables.why: Vomit carries hydrochloric acid, so chloride is lost with the hydrogen ions.

variables.name: Plasma potassium
variables.why: Potassium is lost in the vomit and, as aldosterone rises, in the urine.

variables.name: Blood volume
variables.why: She is losing fluid and taking little in.

variables.name: Aldosterone
variables.why: Low blood volume activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system.

why.correct: Losing bicarbonate-rich intestinal fluid causes a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with high chloride, low potassium and low blood volume. The lungs compensate by lowering PaCO2.

variables.name: Plasma bicarbonate
variables.why: Intestinal fluid is rich in bicarbonate, and it leaves in the stool.

variables.name: Plasma chloride
variables.why: The kidneys and gut keep chloride in place of the lost bicarbonate, so chloride concentration rises.

variables.name: Anion gap
variables.why: Chloride replaces the lost bicarbonate, so Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−) stays about the same.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: Lower bicarbonate lowers the bicarbonate to carbon dioxide ratio.

variables.name: Arterial PaCO2
variables.why: The carotid bodies sense the low pH and speed breathing, which blows off carbon dioxide: respiratory compensation.

variables.name: Plasma potassium
variables.why: Stool water carries potassium, which the colon secretes.

variables.name: Blood volume
variables.why: Water and sodium are lost in stool faster than they are replaced.

why.correct: An acute rise in PaCO2 lowers pH at once, because the kidneys need days to act. Over 3 to 5 days, they excrete more acid and add new bicarbonate, and pH climbs back toward normal while PaCO2 stays high: acute respiratory acidosis becomes partially compensated.

variables.name: PaCO2, first hour
variables.why: Less alveolar ventilation removes carbon dioxide more slowly than his cells make it, so it builds up.

variables.name: Blood pH, first hour
variables.why: More carbon dioxide lowers the bicarbonate to carbon dioxide ratio before the kidneys can respond.

variables.name: PaCO2, five days later
variables.why: His ventilation stays at the same low level, so PaCO2 stays at the same high level.

variables.name: Ammonium in his urine, five days later
variables.why: High PaCO2 acidifies his tubule cells, which secrete more H+ and make more ammonium from glutamine.

variables.name: Plasma bicarbonate, five days later
variables.why: Each H+ excreted on ammonium or phosphate adds a new bicarbonate to his blood: renal compensation.

variables.name: Blood pH, five days later
variables.why: Higher bicarbonate raises the ratio back toward 20, so pH rises toward normal, though usually not all the way.

why.correct: Hyperventilation lowers PaCO2 and causes an acute respiratory alkalosis. Low free calcium explains her tingling and hand spasms, and constricted brain arterioles explain her lightheadedness. Ten minutes is far too short for the kidneys to respond.

variables.name: Arterial PaCO2
variables.why: She breathes out carbon dioxide faster than her cells make it.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: Less carbon dioxide raises the bicarbonate to carbon dioxide ratio.

variables.name: Free calcium in plasma
variables.why: In alkalemia, more calcium binds to albumin, leaving less free.

variables.name: Blood flow to the brain
variables.why: Low carbon dioxide constricts the brain's arterioles, which is why she feels lightheaded.

why.correct: Insulin lack drives both high glucose and ketogenesis. Ketone acids use up bicarbonate and raise the anion gap, the lungs compensate by lowering PaCO2, and glucose in the urine pulls water out, leaving him dehydrated.

variables.name: Blood glucose
variables.why: Without insulin, muscle and fat take up little glucose, and the liver keeps releasing it.

variables.name: Blood ketone bodies
variables.why: Unchecked lipolysis floods the liver with fatty acids, which it turns into ketone bodies faster than tissues can burn them.

variables.name: Plasma bicarbonate
variables.why: Bicarbonate is used up buffering the hydrogen ions the ketone bodies release.

variables.name: Anion gap
variables.why: Ketone body anions, which the test does not measure, take the place of the bicarbonate used up.

variables.name: Ventilation
variables.why: The carotid bodies sense the low arterial pH and drive deep, fast Kussmaul breathing.

variables.name: Arterial PaCO2
variables.why: The extra ventilation blows off carbon dioxide: respiratory compensation.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: Glucose spilling into the urine holds water with it.

why.correct: Vomiting and stomach suction remove hydrochloric acid and leave its matching bicarbonate in the blood. Loop diuretics and excess aldosterone speed H+ and K+ secretion in the collecting duct. Diarrhea causes metabolic acidosis, and an opioid overdose causes respiratory acidosis.
options: Correct. Losing stomach acid leaves the bicarbonate of the alkaline tide in the blood.
Correct. Suction removes stomach acid just as vomiting does.
Correct. The diuretic causes loss of volume, chloride and potassium, and more sodium reaching the collecting duct is traded for H+ and K+.
Diarrhea removes bicarbonate-rich intestinal fluid, causing metabolic acidosis.
Correct. Aldosterone speeds H+ and K+ secretion, so the kidneys add new bicarbonate to the blood.
An opioid overdose depresses breathing and raises PaCO2: respiratory acidosis.

why.correct: Start with the pH, because it tells you what the disorder must explain. Then check PaCO2 and bicarbonate, name the primary disorder from whichever matches the pH, and only then judge whether the other number has moved to compensate.
Hydrogen ions from ketone bodies use up bicarbonate as it buffers them, so plasma bicarbonate falls, not rises. The fall in bicarbonate is what defines a metabolic acidosis.
options: This step is right. Insulin normally restrains lipolysis; without it, fat breakdown runs unchecked.
This step is right. The flood of fatty acids drives ketogenesis in the liver.
This is the error. Bicarbonate takes up the H+ and is used up, so it falls.
This step is right. The carotid bodies sense arterial pH from any cause and drive Kussmaul breathing.
This step is right. Lowering PaCO2 is respiratory compensation; it raises the ratio but does not fully correct the pH.

why.correct: The anion gap is sodium, the main measured cation, minus the two main measured anions, chloride and bicarbonate.
options: Correct. Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−), normally about 8 to 12 mmol/L.
Potassium is a cation, not an anion, and the usual formula leaves it out.
PaCO2 is a gas pressure, not an ion concentration.
Albumin is the main unmeasured anion. It is part of what the gap stands for, not part of the formula.

why.correct: Renal compensation starts within hours but builds over days, as tubule cells step up H+ secretion and ammonium production. Two hours in, only a small rise from buffering has happened.
options: Correct. Renal compensation is slow: full effect takes 3 to 5 days.
Sedatives act on the brain's respiratory centers. They do not block carbonic anhydrase.
The lungs are the source of this problem, so they cannot correct it. Respiratory disorders are compensated by the kidneys.
High PaCO2 makes tubule cells secrete more H+ and keep more bicarbonate, not excrete it.

why.correct: In alkalemia, albumin gives up hydrogen ions and binds more calcium, so free calcium in the plasma falls. Low free calcium makes nerve and muscle membranes more excitable, so they fire on their own: tingling, twitching and spasms.
options: Alkalosis tends to lower plasma potassium, not raise it, and tingling comes from nerves firing too easily, not from blocked signals.
Correct. Less free calcium makes nerves and muscles too excitable.
In respiratory alkalosis carbon dioxide is low, not high. Low carbon dioxide constricts brain arterioles.
The tingling comes on within minutes of hyperventilating and goes when breathing slows, which rules out damage to the nerves.

why.correct: Extra oxygen reverses hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, sending blood to poorly ventilated alveoli, so less carbon dioxide is removed. More oxygen on hemoglobin also lets the blood hold less carbon dioxide at the same PaCO2 (the Haldane effect). Studies show his ventilation falls only a little. Oxygen is given to a target saturation, never withheld.
options: This is the older explanation that many exams still expect. In studies, ventilation falls only slightly and briefly when oxygen is given, so a lost hypoxic drive plays at most a small part.
Short-term oxygen does not damage alveoli or block carbon dioxide diffusion.
Kidneys do not retain carbon dioxide; they adjust bicarbonate, and that takes days.
Correct. Ventilation–perfusion mismatch and the Haldane effect account for most of the rise.

why.correct: High PaCO2 pushes toward acid, and low bicarbonate also pushes toward acid. Compensation always moves the second number in the same direction as the first; here they move in opposite directions, so both are primary. Poor breathing raises PaCO2, and lactic acid from poorly perfused tissues lowers bicarbonate.
options: Renal compensation for a respiratory acidosis would raise bicarbonate, not lower it.
Respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis would lower PaCO2, not raise it.
Correct. Two acidoses together, which is why the pH is so low.
Full compensation needs a pH of 7.35 to 7.45. His is 7.11.

why.correct: Her alkalosis lasted because low volume kept angiotensin II and aldosterone high, low chloride stopped type B intercalated cells from secreting bicarbonate, and low potassium sped H+ secretion. Replacing volume, chloride and potassium removes all three, and her kidneys excrete the extra bicarbonate.
options: Dilution alone would lower bicarbonate only slightly. The large fall comes from the kidneys excreting it.
Correct. Once the causes that keep the kidneys reclaiming bicarbonate are removed, they excrete the excess.
Potassium chloride is a salt, not an acid. It works by replacing lost potassium and chloride.
The lungs remove carbon dioxide, not bicarbonate. Breathing more would raise her pH further.

why.correct: The pH is within range but on the acid side of 7.40. High PaCO2 pushes toward acid and matches that side, so it is the primary disorder. Bicarbonate has risen with it, from days of renal compensation, and the pH is back in range: fully compensated respiratory acidosis.
options: Correct. On exams this is fully compensated; in practice, compensation this complete is uncommon, and a clinician would also consider a second disorder.
Both PaCO2 and bicarbonate are abnormal. A normal pH here reflects compensation, not the absence of a disorder.
A primary metabolic alkalosis would leave the pH on the alkaline side of 7.40. His is 7.37.
Partial compensation leaves the pH outside the normal range. His is inside it.
